How this works

This was not endorsed by any candidate, candidate’s committee, or candidate’s staff. This is not a political advertisement.

These figures show who has returned a ballot so far, not how anyone voted. Party labels come from which primaries a voter chose in past years, and many ballots are redacted, so treat everything here as an early estimate, not a result or a prediction.

Sources
  • Tarrant County’s daily lists of returned mail ballots and of early in-person voters, and its daily totals reports for each. The big number at the top is the county’s own total. The early voting list has no vote dates, so each day’s new names are dated by the county’s daily early voting totals.
  • The county voter file and its 2018–2020 history file, plus older county rosters for the 2022 elections and the 2024 and 2026 primaries.
  • Statewide 2026 primary rosters, for voters who voted in another county.
  • Maps: county voting precincts, city limits, city council and school district maps, and congressional plan C2333.
  • The Census Bureau’s 2020–2024 American Community Survey, including its counts of adult citizens.
  • The county’s 2024 presidential results by precinct, and final turnout for 2018–2024 from the Texas Legislative Council.
  • Past results: the county’s 2022 precinct results for governor, as transcribed by OpenElections, and its archived 2010 and 2014 reports, for ballots by method.
  • Polling locations: the county’s lists of early voting sites and Election Day vote centers, placed on the map with the Census Bureau’s address lookup, and each site’s early-vote totals from the county’s 2018–2024 daily reports, and each vote center’s Election Day count from the county’s 2022 and 2024 reports.
  • Candidates: the Texas Secretary of State’s list of qualified candidates for the Nov. 3 general election, statewide and Tarrant County offices, as of Oct. 11, 2026. Each race lists its candidates by party in alphabetical order (Democratic, Green, Independent, Libertarian, Republican), then write-ins. That is not the order on the ballot. The special elections for Texas Senate District 22 and Texas House District 93 aren’t in that list; they come from the Governor’s proclamations of Aug. 18 and 20, 2026.

Before every update, each number at the top of the page, in the daily chart, the Mail line and the Voters tables is worked out again from the county’s own files and compared with the page, and the page is checked in a browser for broken or out-of-date text. If anything disagrees, the page is not updated.

Early in-person and Election Day ballots are added as the county reports them. On election night, results come from the county’s cumulative and precinct results reports.

Roster Matching
  • Each named ballot is matched to the voter file by its state voter ID. If the ID isn’t on file, a ballot is matched only when the name, middle initial and city point to exactly one person.
  • Older rosters fill in elections the voter file leaves out, and history the county has blanked for some voters.
  • Redacted ballots carry only a precinct and dates. They count in every total and on the map, but never get a party label.
  • If the county’s count runs ahead of its list, the extra ballots show only in the top number, since they have no precinct yet.
Partisanship

A primary ballot shows which party a voter picked that year, not how they’ll vote in November. Five March primaries count: 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2026.

  • Strong: that party at least 4 of 5 times.
  • Mid: 2 or 3 times.
  • Weak: once.
  • Split evenly: both parties equally. Voters who chose both count as weak for the side they chose more often.
  • No party history: general elections only, or no Tarrant history. Presidential voters only are the general-election voters who voted in 2020 or 2024 but in neither midterm (2018, 2022); local and runoff votes don’t change that.
  • Redacted: the county withholds the voter’s name, so there is no history to look up. These count with no party history in the estimate.

Younger voters are judged only on the primaries they were old enough for. A voter with no primary on record but a party label in the voter file (from a 2026 primary runoff, or history the county blanked) counts as weak for that party.

Show the math

For a voter who chose one party in c of the e primaries they were eligible for (old enough: 18 by that November’s Election Day):

strong:c≥2 and ce≥0.8

Weak is c = 1; mid is anything in between. (These are counts of one voter’s primaries, not a sample.)

Electorate Lean and Range

An estimate of how the voters returning ballots lean, not a poll or a forecast of results. Each voter with a Democratic history counts 1 toward Democrats, each with a Republican history 0, and a split record ½.

A ballot with no party history (redacted ones included) counts as the lean that voters with no party history in its precinct showed in the last two Novembers: the precinct’s Democratic share of the vote for governor in 2022 and for president in 2024, minus what its voters with a party history explain, averaged over the two years and pulled toward the county figure in small precincts. Countywide, those voters leaned 48.5% Democratic in 2022 and 46.1% in 2024.

Tested on a past election: built from 2022 alone, this put Tarrant’s 2024 presidential vote at R+3.2 (the result was R+5.2) and came within 3.7 points of a precinct’s margin in half the precincts and within 7.6 points in 80% of them. The March primary share used before version 2.14 gave R+16.1, 14.5 and 21.0.

Areas with few ballots are pulled toward their 2024 presidential result by 8 ballots’ worth, so a handful of voters can’t swing them far; past about 30 ballots this hardly matters.

The range is an 80% range: in 4 of 5 cases these voters’ real lean should fall inside it. It combines how far an electorate can lean from one November to the next (3.5 points), how far the method missed in the 2022-to-2024 test (2 points countywide, 3 for districts, 6 to 14 for precincts by size), and in small areas the luck of which voters have turned out so far. Areas with fewer than 5 ballots show only their counts.

Electorate shift (bottom of the page): the countywide electorate lean and its 80% range for all ballots in through each day, by method, all worked out with the current formula. Mail counts on the day it was received, early in person on the day it was cast. All methods starts 20 days before Election Day; mail starts once 100 ballots were in. Per day shows each day’s ballots on their own (days with at least 100), the dot the day’s estimate and the whisker its range.

Show the mathshare=D+12M+∑i=1Uui+8bN+8

where D = voters with a Democratic history, M = split records, U = ballots with no party history, ui = the no-history lean of the precinct of the i-th of those ballots, b = the area’s 2024 Harris share, and N = all ballots returned so far.

lead=2×share−1range=lead±3.52+m2+e2e=2.56share(1−share)N

with m the test’s miss for that kind of area and e the sampling noise of the ballots so far, all in points. The lean is the Democratic share minus the Republican share, with shares rounded to whole points first, so it is always an even number of points.

Shading
  • Modeled electorate: each area’s lean by voting history, from the formula under Electorate Lean and Range, the same figure its details panel shows. Blue is a Democratic lean, red a Republican lean and white even; darker means a bigger lean. Areas with fewer than 5 ballots stay gray. Diagonal lines mark areas where more than half of the ballots have no party history.
  • March primary result: Democratic minus Republican share of the area’s March 2026 primary ballots.
  • Party history vs. March primary: arrows comparing voters returning ballots with the area’s March primary voters. Left means more Democratic, right more Republican, and a longer arrow is a bigger gap. Areas need at least 5 returning voters with a party history.
  • Party history vs. registered voters: the same arrows against the area’s registered voters with a party history (more Democratic or Republican primaries since 2018, or the voter file’s party label). This shows who is turning out compared with who could, whichever party’s primary was busier. Areas need at least 20 registered voters with a party history.
  • Party history vs. 2024 (president): the same comparison against each area’s 2024 Harris share of the two-party vote. 2024 precincts are moved to today’s areas by where their voters are registered now.
  • Turnout (percentage): ballots cast divided by registered voters (active and suspense).
  • Turnout (raw votes): the number of ballots cast in each area.
  • Votes still expected: a circle in each area, sized by the votes it should still cast before the polls close (see Votes Still Expected).

Districts are built from voting precincts, and each ballot is placed by the district codes the county gives it. Precincts split by a city or district line are approximate.

Show the math

For the comparison arrows, s is the Democratic share (Democratic, plus half of split, over everyone with a party history):

Δ=sreturning−sbaselinelength∝min(|Δ|,0.25)

An arrow’s length grows with the gap and reaches full length at 25 points.

Census Filters

Figures come from Census block groups, split into precincts and districts by how much of each block group’s land falls inside, so small precincts are approximate. Race uses adult citizens, which fits the electorate better than total population. Areas with fewer than 100 adult citizens are never selected.

Show the mathxarea=∑bwbxb

where xb is a block group’s count and wb is the share of its land inside the area.

Turnout
  • Past years use the county’s daily totals for the 2018–2024 November elections (2016 too, for Votes Still Expected). Mail ballots that arrived after Election Day are left off.
  • Ballot returns map: the map, the line under it and each area’s panel count every ballot in through the day on the slider, or only that day’s ballots with “That day” (mail by the day the county received it, early in person by the day it was cast). A single day is a small sample, so more areas fall under the small-number rules.
  • Polling locations: circle area shows each site’s ballots through the day on the slider, or on that day alone with “That day” (sized against the busiest single day at any site). The 1, 2 and 3 marks and each site’s panel follow the slider.
  • The turnout bar marks final turnout in 2018, 2022 and 2024.
  • Pace on All methods adds Election Day in person as one point on Election Day: for 2022 and 2024 (and 2026, once posted) the county’s Election Day Voting Totals; for 2018 and 2020, which have no county Election Day total on file, final turnout minus early in-person and mail ballots, so those two also include provisional ballots. An area’s 2022 and 2024 Election Day is its share of that year’s Election Day voters, from the same precinct lists as mail and early.
  • Pace by area: pick a district, city or school district under AREA (precincts are too small to chart by day). Its 2026 lines count the voters the county lists by name, placed where they are registered now; redacted ballots and the few voters who can’t be matched are left out, so areas add up to a little less than the county. No daily counts exist by area for past years, so an area compares with 2022 and 2024 only, as estimates marked “~” and rounded: the area’s share of that year’s countywide mail, early in-person and Election Day votes, from the county’s list of who voted in each precinct (a precinct split by today’s lines is divided by where its voters that year are registered now), spread over the county’s daily totals. 2018 and 2020 aren’t shown for areas: there is no list of those years’ voters by precinct to place them in today’s districts. A past line’s end point is the area’s share of the real total; its day-to-day shape is the county’s. Mail received more than 20 days out counts in the running total but isn’t shown day by day. For an area, the turnout bar shows 2026 only.
  • No mail arrives on Sundays and federal holidays, and the county doesn’t always count on weekends, so lines go flat and then jump.
Votes Still Expected

A projection of how many more votes each area should cast before the polls close on Nov. 3. It is not a count, and it says nothing about party. It updates with each early voting and mail report.

  • Early in person: the count so far divided by the share of early voting that past Novembers (2016, 2018, 2022 and 2024) had cast by the same day of the period, taking the middle of the four results (the median). Predicting each of those years from the other three, this missed the full early vote by 2.9% on average at day 4 and 4.3% at day 5, and by under 3% on average from day 10 on.
  • Mail: ballots sent times the share of sent ballots that came back by Election Day in 2018, 2020 and 2022 (about 80%). Tested on those years 11 days out, this missed by 4% or less; the return curve used before missed by up to 22%.
  • Election Day: a share of registered voters. In 2018 and 2022 it held at 14.28% (161,855 and 180,249 ballots) while early voting grew from 31% to 38% of registered voters. In 2010 and 2014, with far less early voting, it was 19.2% and 16.2%, and in the presidential years it fell about 0.57 points for each point of early voting. Early voting in 2026 is heading past every past midterm, so the rule takes the middle of the two: 14.28%, and 14.28% less 0.57 times the early share beyond 2018’s. Its range is plus or minus 12%.
  • By area: every registered voter who hasn’t voted yet gets a chance of voting from their own record (past general elections and primaries, age, how long they’ve been registered, and active or suspense status). Each chance is adjusted for how much of that voter’s likely ballot is already due, given how they voted in 2022 and 2024, and for how far ahead of or behind its usual pace their precinct is running (to the 0.6 power, fitted on this year’s daily early voting lists). The chances are then scaled to the countywide total, split by method, and added up by area.
  • The 80% range combines the countywide range with the error measured when this method predicted 2022 by precinct: about 7 to 8% for districts; for precincts, 10% with 800 or more expected voters, 22% with 300 to 800, 28% with 150 to 300, and about 47% under 150. Precincts under 150 expected voters say the estimate is rough.
  • Each tab shows its own part: All methods, everything until the polls close; Early in person, the rest of early voting (through Oct. 30); Election Day; Mail, mail ballots still to come. “Already cast” compares the ballots in so far with those plus the ones still expected.
  • Thanks to Tyler McVety, whose early-vote nowcast informed the comparison with past years’ daily patterns.
Show the math

Early in person, after k days with c votes so far, where sy(k) is the share of year y’s early vote cast by day k:

E=caverage of sy(k)

A voter with chance p of voting, who hasn’t voted yet, with share q of their likely ballot already due, in a precinct running at r times its expected pace:

pstill=p(1−q)1−pq×r0.6

All voters’ chances are moved up or down together until they add up to the countywide figure.

Election Night
  • The county’s first report, due by 7:15 p.m., has countywide totals for mail and early in-person votes only. Election Day votes are added through the night, and precinct-by-precinct results follow.
  • From 7 p.m., results come first. A Results section opens the page with the county’s latest report (its time, precincts reporting and ballots counted), cards for the U.S. Senate, Governor and County Judge races (tap one to show it on the map), and lists of every race with each candidate’s votes. Who voted (ballots cast, the named voters and the electorate lean) stays right under it. The Mail, Early in person and Election Day tabs show the votes cast that way.
  • Until the county posts its Election Day turnout, ballots cast adds the Election Day ballots counted so far, and the Election Day tab shows that count on its own. It is the most ballots any one race was counted on in the county’s latest report: its votes, undervotes and overvotes.
  • Once the county posts its Election Day roster (the voters who checked in at a vote center), the map, the tables, the electorate lean and each area’s panel count those voters too, matched to their voting history the same way as the mail and early voting lists. The roster and the results are separate county files, so their Election Day counts can differ slightly; the line under the big number gives both.
  • Until precinct results are posted, district panels (Congress, Texas House and Senate, State Board of Education, Commissioner, Justice of the Peace) show their race’s Tarrant County totals. Once they are posted, the map is shaded by the party lead and every panel shows its races. Cities, council districts and school districts cut through precincts, so their figures are estimates and say so.
  • The estimates and daily snapshots from before results stay on the map: under Modeled electorate, in each panel under “Estimate before results,” in the Shading menu and on the snapshot slider.
  • Above the map, Map shows switches between Results (each area shaded by the party lead in the race picked under Race on the map), Modeled electorate (the estimate from the voters’ party history) and Comparison. Comparison draws an arrow in each area for the gap between the results and what you pick under Results compared with: the modeled electorate, the 2024 vote for president, registered voters’ party history or the March primary. Left means the results were more Democratic, right more Republican. Its length is the gap between the two leads, full length at 50 points or more, and each area’s panel gives both leads. The model needs 5 ballots in an area, and the others need 20 votes for president, 20 registered voters with a party history or 20 primary ballots. Results are shown as the county publishes them, however few the votes.
  • No race calls. This website will not update races as called until the results have been certified by the county, which may take multiple days or weeks. Until then, candidates are listed in party order, never by who is ahead, and nothing is marked as won.
  • Before results go up, every race total is checked against the county’s report and every district against its own precincts. A report that can’t be read or doesn’t add up is not posted, and the page keeps the last one that did.
Limitations
  • A primary choice is not a November vote. People cross over, and many November voters skip primaries.
  • Most mail voters are 65 or older, so early numbers lean older than the full electorate.
  • Redacted ballots and voters who skip primaries add no party information, which is why the range is wide.
  • When the county blanks a voter’s history, older rosters restore most of it, but a few voters may sit one tier too low.
  • Small areas can swing a lot on a few ballots.
  • The electorate lean assumes voters with no party history lean the way such voters in their precinct did in 2022 and 2024. A year that moves them differently moves the estimate with it.
  • Votes still expected follows past patterns. An unusual year can miss, most of all on Election Day and in small precincts.
Privacy and Freedom of Information
  • In Texas, voter files and lists of who voted early or returned a mail ballot are public records that anyone can request. They show whether someone voted and which primary they chose, never how they voted. Ballots are secret.
  • No names or addresses appear on this site. It shows only counts for precincts, districts and the county.
  • The page holds totals, not individual ballots: counts for each precinct and day by party history, and separate counts by age, sex and registration period. A count of 1 or 2 shows as “<3”, and an area with fewer than 3 ballots shows no breakdown, estimate or map color. Election results are different: they are the county’s own published counts, shown as published, small numbers too.
  • Ballots the county redacts stay unidentified.
  • Votes still expected are rounded projections for areas, never tied to a person. Under 5 shows as “fewer than 5.”
Disclosure

Every record comes directly from official government sources (Tarrant County Elections Administration, the Texas Secretary of State, the Texas Legislative Council, the U.S. Census Bureau, the cities of Fort Worth, Arlington, and Grand Prairie, and Fort Worth ISD). The one exception: the county’s 2022 precinct results come from OpenElections’ transcription of its report. The records are analyzed as published, with nothing added, altered, or invented.

While the gathering of records and the design mockups are organic, Claude was used to write the code that sorts and analyzes the data, and to code with the mockups to assist in UI/UX development, using Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, GeoPandas, Shapely, openpyxl), Poppler, matplotlib, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Given the water, energy, and carbon footprint of using AI, donations will be made to organizations working to hold AI and data center developers accountable for their use of precious resources.
